source.title: The power of quantum neural networks
source.authors: Amira Abbas; David Sutter; Christa Zoufal; Aurélien Lucchi; A. Figalli; S. Woerner

record.tranche_reason: The study investigates quantum and classical model capacity and trainability, but does not test any listed version about natural-label generalization, the mapped architecture/optimizer/batch/regularization conditions, magnitude-aware sharpness, or memorized-example removal.
record.gate_note: Appendix B.2 reports effective dimension as label randomization increases, but does not report held-out error for that experiment. Iris results report training loss only. Figure 6 values are not stated numerically. No cited prior-work findings are recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures effective dimension, Fisher spectra and training loss, and proves a generalization bound. It reports no held-out performance or magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization-gap comparison that tests V1–V8. Fitting corrupted labels alone does not test V1's coexistence claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors present effective dimension as a capacity measure justified by a generalization bound and the label-corruption experiment. Their main conclusion is that a suitably designed quantum network has higher effective dimension and faster training than comparable classical and easy-feature-map quantum models. They leave generalization performance across datasets and larger models for future work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a Fisher-information-based effective-dimension analysis and quantum-versus-classical model experiments, rather than the natural-label generalization interventions or measurements in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature-map choice changes the Fisher-information spectrum and the reported trainability properties of the quantum models.

fits_no_version.finding: For a single-hidden-layer network with 880 weights trained to zero training loss on 1,000 make-blobs examples, effective dimension increases with label randomization; Figure 6 averages 10 training runs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effective dimension increases with label corruption in this synthetic classification setting; the authors interpret this as evidence of its usefulness as a capacity measure.

record.problems: Appendix B.2's generalization analysis reports effective dimension but no held-out error values. The text gives no exact Figure 6 values. The hardware training experiment was run once, and the authors note that noise analysis and repeated initializations would make it more robust; that experiment measures training loss, not the listed generalization claims.
record.rows_left_out: The Iris simulator comparison in Figure 3b and Table 1 reports training loss and Fisher-Rao norm, not held-out performance or a listed version's measure, so it was not entered as a row.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting with above-chance natural-label held-out accuracy and chance random-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and training recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification test error and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer held-out performance under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out error across dataset sizes, dropout strengths and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness ranking measured training–test gaps and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Test accuracy after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Fisher-spectrum flatness and effective dimension are not V7's magnitude-aware sharpness measure. The Iris experiments compare training loss, with no held-out evaluation; using Adam and full batches supplies no optimizer or batch-size comparison.

versions.untested_parts: Natural-label held-out performance compared with random-label chance performance after fitting random labels.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
Image test-error comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks and the role of local connectivity.
Held-out performance comparison of adaptive and non-adaptive optimizers.
Large-batch versus small-batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Effect of dropout on held-out error across training-set sizes and dropout strengths.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its relation to the training–test gap.
Effect on test accuracy of removing memorized training examples and retraining.

rows.subject: feedforward neural network with a single hidden layer
rows.size_stated: input size sin = 6, output size sout = 2, number of trainable weights d = 880; 1000 data points
rows.operation_detail: Calculated effective dimension after training to zero training loss on confusion sets with increasingly randomised labels.
rows.value: The effective dimension increases as the data becomes more random; exact values are figure only.
rows.uncertainty: one standard deviation above and below the mean
rows.note: The experiment describes the measure's trend as labels are randomised; it does not report held-out error or a measured training–test gap.
rows.check: The reported increase in effective dimension is correctly extracted, but it cannot establish any listed version's effect. Appendix B.2 reports zero training loss across the considered confusion sets without measuring natural-label held-out accuracy or random-label held-out chance performance.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
